Design to be implemented based on certain events in the process:
![aio-loading-mockup-vs1](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/2958442/25460315/a1ba93d8-2a97-11e7-9e9b-68442464e9cc.png)

The `http` library does not support progress out of the box. So to display this loader with meaninful progress will require one of three things:

a) install and use a 3rd party adapter for `http` library: e.g. https://github.com/DarkXaHTeP/angular-progress-http
b) ditch `http` and use barebones APIs, such as `fetch` or `XHR`, directly
c) wait for @alxhub to release `HttpClient` to us (perhaps as an early preview?)
We could at least show an indeterminate progress bar (until the new HttpClient is usable).

@wardbell I spoke with @petebacondarwin and he suggested that we use the indeterminet progress bar from material: https://material.angular.io/components/component/progress-bar I'm totally fine with this and it simplifies the implementation quite a bit since we don't need to worry about progress points to tie the animations to. I think this is a good idea.

can you use the placement that @sjtrimble suggested, but use the material progress bar.

closes #16110
## Jank Nightmares - _UPDATE: Everything is fixed_

I'm using absolute positioning which I thought meant that the `<md-progress-bar>` in `app.component.html` would not take space. But I cannot stop the content area from bobbing during/after progress. Interestingly the side-nav and TOC panel don't jump. Only the main content area.

We should only see the bar if there is going to be an appreciable delay.
This implementation won't reveal the progress bar _at all_ if the time from location change to doc render is brief (see use of `setTimeout` and `isFetchingId` in  `app.component.ts).

It can be hard to see what's going on when running on a desktop browser. One approach I took is to add a 2sec delay to doc.json fetching in the `document.service`.
